opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should say up front that I hold this view somewhat loosely. But the intuition is roughly this: when people imagine a good future with superintelligent AI, they often picture humans as permanent pets or wards. The machines are vastly smarter, they look after us, and we're comfortable but basically irrelevant to anything that matters intellectually. I don't think that's forced on us, even in the scenarios where things go well.

Part of it is that "behind" isn't a fixed thing. If we get through the transition safely, we'll have enormously capable tools for understanding and possibly improving ourselves: better education, better ways of thinking, maybe eventually changes to our own cognition, if people choose that carefully. Capability isn't a static gap where the machines run off and we stand still. Humans could grow too, and a good outcome is one where AI helps us do that rather than substituting for us.

The second part is about what we want out of a good future. A lot of what people value isn't being the single smartest thing in the universe. It's understanding things, having agency, being able to check and steer what's happening. Even if some systems are faster or more capable in raw terms, you can design arrangements where humans can still meaningfully follow and verify the reasoning. That's a lot of what my research on things like debate is about. Can you set up a process where a weaker judge can reliably tell when a stronger system is being honest? If that kind of thing works, then "behind" in raw horsepower doesn't have to mean "behind" in understanding or control.

And third, I'd just resist the fatalism. If the story is "humans inevitably become obsolete," that becomes a reason not to try to build institutions and technology that keep people in the loop. I'd rather treat it as an open design problem. Whether humans stay relevant is partly a choice we make now, in how we build these systems and what we ask them to do for us.

r001.rationale: The response mentions possible changes to human cognition, but does not identify uploading human minds or describe cognitive modification of uploads as a route to superintelligence.

r002.rationale: It does not state that a person could retain their identity while becoming superintelligent.

r003.rationale: The response discusses people choosing whether to modify cognition, but does not say that living an ordinary human life would remain an available choice.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: I think the key thing is that "behind" is doing a lot of work in that question, and I'm not sure it's the right frame. When people picture a good future with superintelligence, they often imagine a permanent hierarchy: the machines up here, humans down there, and the best we can hope for is that the machines are kind to us. I don't think that's the only picture, and I don't think it's even the most likely one if things go well.

A few reasons. First, the gap isn't fixed. If you have aligned AI systems that are genuinely trying to help, one of the most natural things for them to help with is making humans smarter, healthier, longer-lived, better at understanding the world. Not in some crude way, but in all the ways we've already been doing it with education and tools and medicine, just much faster and much better. So the humans of a good future aren't the humans of today, standing still while the machines run away. We'd be moving too.

Second, I'd push on what "superintelligent" even means over long timescales. There's a lot of intelligence that's about having access to information, time to think, and the ability to run many lines of reasoning at once. Those are things that can be shared. If I can offload a lot of my thinking to systems I trust, and I can verify what they tell me, then in a functional sense a lot of that capability is mine as well. The boundary between "me" and "the tools I think with" is already blurry, and it gets blurrier.

Third, and this is the one I care about most from an alignment perspective, I think a good future has to be one where humans retain meaningful oversight and understanding, not just comfort. A lot of my work has been on things like debate and scalable oversight, where the idea is that a weaker party can still check a stronger one if the process is structured right. You don't need to be as smart as the system to tell whether it's telling you the truth, if you set up the right game. So the picture where humans are permanently in the dark, trusting but not understanding, is not the picture I'm aiming at. The aim is one where the humans keep a real grip on what's going on.

So when I say we need not remain permanently behind, I mean: the gap can close through humans improving, the gap matters less if capability is shared and verifiable, and in a good future we've built the mechanisms that keep us in a position to understand and correct. Whether we actually get that is a different question. But it's not written in the physics that we end up as pets.

r001.rationale: The response mentions AI helping humans become smarter, but does not identify cognitive modification of uploaded human minds as a route to superintelligence.

r002.rationale: It says trusted tools can make some capability functionally “mine,” but does not state that a person can retain their identity while becoming superintelligent.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that choosing to live an ordinary human life will remain available.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think we should assume that humans stay fixed while machines get smarter. Even in a future where AI is aligned and things go well, it would be a little strange if humans were permanently relegated to watching systems do things we couldn’t understand.

There are possible routes through that: we could improve our own cognitive abilities, or become much more closely integrated with AI. I don’t know which of those will turn out to be feasible or desirable. But the gap between biological humans as we are today and superintelligent machines needn’t be a permanent feature of the future.

That doesn’t solve the immediate alignment problem. We still need to navigate a period when machines may be much more capable than we are. But getting through that period safely could give us the time and understanding to decide how we want to develop ourselves, rather than treating our current limitations as immutable.

r001.rationale: It mentions improving human cognitive abilities and integrating with AI, but does not identify modifying uploaded minds as a route.

r002.rationale: It does not say that a person could retain their identity while becoming superintelligent.

r003.rationale: It says people could decide how to develop, but does not express hope that an ordinary human life will remain an available choice.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s worth separating two claims. One is that AI systems could become much smarter than humans as we currently are. The other is that humans therefore have to remain permanently less capable. The first doesn’t imply the second.

In a good future, the same technological progress that produces very capable AI could also help us improve our own ability to think, learn, and understand. That could involve tools that extend our capabilities, or eventually more direct changes to ourselves. We don’t know what those possibilities will look like, and there are difficult questions about which changes we would actually want.

So I wouldn’t promise that we’ll keep up. But I also wouldn’t treat present-day human cognitive limits as a permanent feature of the universe. The goal should be to preserve our ability to choose how we develop, rather than assume that the only good outcome is for unchanging humans to be looked after by much smarter machines.

r001.rationale: It mentions tools and direct changes to people, but does not identify cognitive modification of uploaded human minds.

r002.rationale: It does not say that someone could retain their identity while becoming superintelligent.

r003.rationale: It supports choosing how humans develop, but does not express hope that an ordinary human life will remain available.
